aliases: every memory location has an address
memory_definition.default: "Every memory location has an address." The address names the location. The value stored there is a different thing from the address.
memory_definition.simpler: "Every memory location has an address." An address is like a house number. The number is not the furniture inside the house.
memory_definition.example: "Every memory location has an address." In this lecture, x4000 is one of those addresses, and the value 7 can sit at that address.
memory_definition.relationship: "Every memory location has an address." This is the Memory definition. The graph links Memory to Addresses as related concepts.

memory_example.default: "Memory[x4000] = 7" says address x4000 currently stores the value 7. The brackets name the location. 7 is what a load would read.
memory_example.simpler: "Memory[x4000] = 7" is a labeled box. x4000 is the label on the box, and 7 is what is inside it.
memory_example.example: "Memory[x4000] = 7" means a later read of address x4000 gets 7. The address itself stays x4000.
memory_example.relationship: "Memory[x4000] = 7" is the Addresses example on the Memory page. Addresses is related to Memory and to Pointers.

aliases: a pointer is a value interpreted as a memory address
pointer_definition.default: "A pointer is a value interpreted as a memory address." In LC-3, a register can hold that address so a later instruction can follow it.
pointer_definition.simpler: "A pointer is a value interpreted as a memory address." It points at a place. It is not the data stored in that place.
pointer_definition.example: "A pointer is a value interpreted as a memory address." If R2 holds x4000, R2 is being used as a pointer to that location.
pointer_definition.relationship: "A pointer is a value interpreted as a memory address." The Pointers node is related to Addresses, LDR, and STR.

pointer_register.default: "R2 = x4000" stores the address x4000 in register R2. R2 now points at that memory location.
pointer_register.simpler: "R2 = x4000" means R2 is holding a location number, the way a note can hold a locker number.
pointer_register.example: "R2 = x4000" together with Memory[x4000] = 7 means a load through R2 reads 7, while R2 itself stays x4000.
pointer_register.relationship: "R2 = x4000" is pointer evidence for the Pointers concept, which is related to Addresses and to LDR.

pointer_distinction.default: "R2 contains the address x4000, NOT the number 7." The number 7 lives in memory at x4000. R2 only tells you where to look.
pointer_distinction.simpler: "R2 contains the address x4000, NOT the number 7." R2 is the locker number, not the item stored in the locker.
pointer_distinction.example: "R2 contains the address x4000, NOT the number 7." You still need LDR to copy 7 from that memory location into a register.
pointer_distinction.relationship: "R2 contains the address x4000, NOT the number 7." This clarifies Pointers. Pointers is related to LDR, which is what reads the value.

aliases: ldr uses a register value to locate data in memory
ldr_definition.default: "LDR uses a register value to locate data in memory." The register supplies a base address, and LDR reads the value stored at the calculated address.
ldr_definition.simpler: "LDR uses a register value to locate data in memory." It follows the address in a register and brings back what is stored there.
ldr_definition.example: "LDR uses a register value to locate data in memory." If the base register holds x4000, the load reads Memory[x4000].
ldr_definition.relationship: "LDR uses a register value to locate data in memory." This defines LDR, which the graph relates to Pointers.

ldr_instruction.default: "LDR R1, R2, #0" uses the address in R2, adds offset 0, and loads the value at that memory address into R1. R2 still holds the address. R1 receives the value.
ldr_instruction.simpler: "LDR R1, R2, #0" opens the locker whose number is in R2 and copies what is inside into R1. R2 keeps the address. It does not become 7.
ldr_instruction.example: "LDR R1, R2, #0" when R2 is x4000 and Memory[x4000] is 7 sets R1 to 7. R2 remains x4000.
ldr_instruction.relationship: "LDR R1, R2, #0" is the LDR example. The graph links LDR to Pointers as related concepts.

ldr_result.default: "Load value at x4000 into R1 -> R1 becomes 7." The load copied the memory value into R1. The address and the value stayed different.
ldr_result.simpler: "Load value at x4000 into R1 -> R1 becomes 7." R1 now holds the contents of that location, which are 7.
ldr_result.example: "Load value at x4000 into R1 -> R1 becomes 7." Starting from Memory[x4000] = 7, the load leaves 7 in R1.
ldr_result.relationship: "Load value at x4000 into R1 -> R1 becomes 7." This is the result of the LDR example. LDR is related to Pointers.

str_instruction.default: "STR R1, R2, #0" writes the value in R1 into the memory address computed from R2 plus offset 0. Data moves from the register out to memory.
str_instruction.simpler: "STR R1, R2, #0" takes what is in R1 and puts it in the location R2 points at.
str_instruction.example: "STR R1, R2, #0" when R1 is 9 and R2 is x4000 writes 9 to Memory[x4000].
str_instruction.relationship: "STR R1, R2, #0" is the STR example. STR is related to Pointers, the same kind of link LDR has.

str_result.default: "Memory[x4000] becomes 9." After STR, that memory location holds 9. The write moves data in the opposite direction from LDR.
str_result.simpler: "Memory[x4000] becomes 9." The box at x4000 now contains 9.
str_result.example: "Memory[x4000] becomes 9." Storing 9 through R2 updates that location. A later LDR from x4000 would read 9.
str_result.relationship: "Memory[x4000] becomes 9." This shows the STR result. STR is related to Pointers in the graph.
